opus-5.5.text:
I think the shift happened quite naturally, and honestly it came from a feeling of dissatisfaction.

Early on, like many people in computer vision at that time, I was working in a very benchmark-driven way. You pick a task, say face recognition or detection, find a dataset, design a module, and push the number up by one or two points. That kind of work has real value. It trains you to be rigorous and to care about details. But after a while I started asking: what did the model actually learn? If the accuracy goes from 95 to 96, do I understand the problem better, or have I just found a better way to fit this particular dataset?

That question led me toward representations. Whatever task a network solves, the real work happens in the intermediate features. If those representations are good, structured, meaningful, and transferable, many downstream tasks become easy. If they're poor, you're just patching things up task by task.

Generative models were a big turning point for me. When I started working on GANs, I found it fascinating that a network trained only to synthesize realistic images, with no labels at all, ended up with a latent space where directions corresponded to things like age, pose, expression, or lighting. Nobody told the model these concepts existed, yet they emerged. That was a strong signal that a generative objective can produce very rich representations, and that we can study and interpret them, not just use them as a black box.

So much of my work around then, interpreting latent spaces, editing semantics, and inverting real images back into the generator, was really about one question: what has the model learned, and how can we make it useful and controllable?

Looking back, I'd describe it as moving from "how do I win on this benchmark" to "what is a good representation of the visual world, and how do we learn it." Benchmarks are still useful as a measuring stick, but they aren't the goal. The goal is understanding, and representation is where understanding lives inside these models.

r003.rationale: The response asks what models have learned and emphasizes representation learning, but does not explain that difficulty understanding how to improve generative models motivated that shift.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it wasn't a clean, planned transition. When I started my PhD, the field was very benchmark-driven. You pick a task, say face recognition or image classification, you look at the leaderboard, and you try to push the number up by a point or two. I did that for a while, and I learned a lot from it, because benchmarks force you to be rigorous. But after a couple of papers I started to feel a kind of emptiness. You beat the previous method, you get the paper accepted, and then six months later someone beats you by another half a point. Nobody really understood why the model worked. We were tuning architectures and tricks, not understanding anything.

The turning point for me was when I started playing with generative models, GANs in particular. I was supposed to be working on something practical, but I got curious about a simple question: what does the model actually know? If a GAN can synthesize realistic bedrooms or faces, somewhere inside those layers it must have encoded concepts like lighting, pose, gender, whether there is a window in the room. So I started poking at the latent space, moving along directions and seeing what changed. And it turned out that a lot of those concepts were there, linearly, without anyone ever labeling them. That felt completely different from benchmark chasing. It was the first time I felt like I was discovering something about the model rather than just competing with other people's models.

Once you see that, you can't unsee it. The question stops being "how do I get a higher score" and becomes "what representation is this model learning, and can we control it, reuse it, interpret it." That naturally pulls you toward representation learning. And the beautiful thing is that this question doesn't belong to any single task. The same representation might serve editing, recognition, 3D understanding, whatever. So in a sense I didn't leave benchmarks behind, I just realized they were measuring the output of something much more interesting that nobody was looking at directly.

I'd also say the timing mattered. Around that period, self-supervised learning and large pretrained models were taking off, and the whole community was shifting from "train a model for one task" to "learn a good representation once, then adapt." So my personal curiosity happened to line up with where the field was going. I'd like to claim foresight, but a lot of it was just following what I found interesting and being lucky that the field moved in the same direction.

astra-6.text:
For me, it was a gradual shift from asking, “How can we improve performance on this task?” to asking, “What has the model actually learned that makes that performance possible?” With computer vision benchmarks, you have a concrete objective, and that’s useful. But a better score doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the model has learned something general or something very specific to that benchmark.

That led me toward representation learning. I became more interested in how a model organizes visual information—what it preserves, what it ignores, and whether those features can support different tasks. The benchmark is still important, but it becomes a way to examine the representation rather than the whole purpose of the research.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was a gradual shift from asking, “How can we solve this particular task better?” to asking, “What has the model actually learned?” With computer vision benchmarks, you have a clear task and a metric, which makes progress easy to measure. But the score alone doesn’t tell you much about how the model represents the visual world.

I became more interested in that underlying representation: what information it captures, how that information is organized, and whether it can support different tasks. Generative models offer a particularly interesting way to explore those questions. You can change something inside the model and observe how the generated image changes, which gives you a way to investigate what the representation means.

So I see it less as leaving computer vision behind and more as looking underneath the individual tasks, trying to understand the representations that make those capabilities possible.
